 Yoga-related practice could help veterans, others with sleep disorders

 Facebook

 Photo by RDNE Stock project
 By Paul Mackarey PUBLISHED: November 1, 2026 at 12:00 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... First of two parts.
 Veterans Day has been a federal holiday since 1938 — although it was called Armistice Day until 1954 — intended to honor with gratitude those members of the armed forces who sacrificed for our freedom. What better way to remember these men and women than by looking out for their health?
 Many veterans have suffered greatly — mentally and physically — from their service. Sleep disorders, often associated with other mental and physical problems, are among the most common maladies. In fact, about 40% of United States veterans report problems with sleep, compared to 30% of adults overall.
 According to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data, nearly 13% of American adults said they had used some type of sleep aid every day or most days in the past month. That includes prescription medications, over-the-counter medications and supplements, and marijuana or CBD products.
 It’s a familiar predicament: Your eyes are heavy, your body hurts and you finally crawl into bed, but despite being completely exhausted, your brain has decided that now is the appropriate time to think about everything. Something that’s happening tomorrow. Something you forgot to do yesterday. Something you said five years ago. The grocery list. That one weird noise in the house.
 Sleep, unfortunately, is not always as simple as being tired.
 Sleep is important to overall mental and physical health and well-being. While you sleep, your body is still working. Sleep supports memory, immune function, metabolism and recovery.
 Researchers are also continuing to learn more about how sleep may help the brain clear metabolic waste products. A recent review in the journal Physiology looked at the relationship between sleep and the brain’s glymphatic clearance system, which is involved in moving metabolic waste out of brain tissue. Sleep, particularly deeper stages of sleep, appears to play an important role in this process. Your brain does not just shut off for the night. It changes gears.
 New research in the area of sleep is encouraging. Richard Miller, Ph.D., an American clinical psychologist, is working with veterans and active-duty military personnel practicing integrative restoration, or iRest, a modern adaptation of the ancient practice of yoga nidra. His work has been studied in military and veteran populations, including people experiencing symptoms related to post-traumatic stress disorder.
 In one feasibility study, veterans with combat-related PTSD participated in iRest and described improvements in areas including relaxation and well-being. But larger studies are still needed.
 How it works
 The beauty of iRest is that it does not ask you to force yourself to sleep; it asks you to lie down and rest.
 Yoga nidra is often translated as “yogic sleep,” but it is not meant to replace actual sleep. Think of it more as guided deep relaxation that incorporates some of the principles of progressive muscle relaxation. You lie comfortably, usually with your eyes closed, and listen to someone guide your attention through different areas of your body.
 If your mind is already racing, the idea of trying to guide yourself through relaxation can feel like just one more chore. But it doesn’t work out that way.
 An audible voice gives your mind something gentle to follow. You might begin at your toes and simply notice them, letting them soften. Move into the feet and ankles, slowly up the shins, over the knees and through the thighs. Let your hips settle, your pelvis, your abdomen rise and fall with each breath. There is nothing you need to hold in right now.
 Let your shoulders sink into whatever is holding you — the bed, the floor, the couch. Allow your neck to lengthen as it rests. Notice the back of your head, your chin and your jaw. Feel the space around your shoulder blades, then move your attention to your ears, temples and forehead. And then slowly, almost without trying, release through the eyelids. Let your tongue release from the top of your mouth, allowing your lips to gently part.
 Maybe you’ll fall asleep. Maybe you won’t. Either way, your body has had an opportunity to stop bracing for a minute.
 Yoga nidra and iRest are not replacements for sleep or medical care, or a treatment for PTSD. Meditating may not be comfortable for everyone, particularly some people with trauma. But as a nondrug approach to relaxation, guided meditation may be another option worth exploring for people who struggle to settle down at night.
 Guest contributor Shelby Yeakel is a physical therapist assistant and doctor of physical therapy student at Mackarey Physical Therapy. She is a certified yoga instructor and served in the Marine Corps from 2014 to 2017. 
 Paul J. Mackarey, P.T., D.H.Sc., is a doctor in health sciences specializing in orthopedic and sports physical therapy. He is in private practice in Scranton and Clarks Summit and is an associate professor of clinical medicine at Geisinger Commonwealth School of Medicine. Email: mackareypt@gmail.com.
